newsitem.title: GERMANY: Greenpeace in multi-country protest over gene soya.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace in multi-country protest over gene soya.

text.p: The environmentalist group Greenpeace on Wednesday said it had coordinated protests in a number of European countries against genetically-modified soybeans from the United States.
Greenpeace said in a statement it planned an action later on Monday in the U.S., where the soya is being harvested, but gave no details.
It wants to have the imports blocked or to see the soybeans specially labelled.

"We've got activists trying to stick banners on Unilever buildings in Germany, Britain, Sweden and the Netherlands and there will be a press conference in Switzerland showing wholesale traders there are asking for segregation of the beans in the U.S.," said local Greenpeace co-ordinator Michael Kuehn.
Anglo-Dutch food manufacturer Unilever has been targeted by the group as a leading consumer of soya products.

About 50 Greenpeace demonstrators protested outside Unilever's London headquarters, protesting that consumers had no way of avoiding the genetically-altered beans, developed by Monsanto Co to be resistant to a weed-killer.
A Unilever spokesman in London said the U.S., UK and European authorities had declared the beans safe and Unilever had come to the same conclusion after making its own assessment.
But Greenpeace said it had not been proven that there was no danger of allergic reactions or heightened immunity to antibiotics from traces of gene-altered organisms.
Sticking colourful banners reading "Do you want your food genetically-manipulated?" and "No to gene soya in food" to the Unilever building in Hamburg proved difficult because of rain, Kuehn said.
He said the organisation had chosen October 16 for its protest because it was United Nations World Food Day.
Unilever said it was not possible to separate out the genetically-modified beans or label products using them.
But Kuehn said, "There are tests available and there are suppliers of non-gene-altered soybeans in the U.S. and Europe."
"We demand from the food multis that at least they will clarify where they got their raw materials and whether they have been genetically-modified."

Greenpeace said it had a list of supermarket and wholesale organisations in Austria, Switzerland, Sweden and Norway which would not stock products containing genetically-engineered soya unless they were separated and labelled.
A number of German, Belgian and Dutch firms had committed themselves to the same goals earlier, Greenpeace said.
